blocks.text: The mole is deservedly counted among the unclean animals in the Law, since it neither divides the hoof nor chews the cud. Moreover, by its blindness it is a type of those whose minds the god of this world has blinded, lest the splendour of the Gospel should dawn upon them, 2 Cor. IV, 4. And while it is continually busy digging in the earth, it represents those men who care for nothing but earthly things, Philipp. III, 19. and whose wisdom is earthly, sensual, devilish, Iacobi III, 15. But the weasel (mustela), which the interpreters have hitherto wanted to be designated by the word חולד choled, signifies, as Cyril taught us above (as emended by us), τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφοδεῆ τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [ta deila, kai ananda, kai psophodeē tōn kleptōn genē]. Of the same sort is that in Aristeas: Κακοποιητικὸς ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos ho tropos esti kai galēs, kai myōn]; Mischievous are the habits both of the weasel and of mice. And a little later: Τότε τῆς γαλῆς γένος ἰδιάζον ἐστί. χωρὶς γὰρ τοῦ προειρημένου, ἔχει λυμαντικὸν κατάστημα· διὰ γὰρ τῶν ὤτων συλλαμβάνει, τεκνοποιεῖ δὲ τῷ στόματι [Tote tēs galēs genos idiazon esti. chōris gar tou proeirēmenou, echei lymantikon katastēma; dia gar tōn ōtōn syllambanei, teknopoiei de tō stomati]. Which in the Hebrew runs thus: הנה עוד בסגולת טבעו התועבה הזאת שהנקבה תהר מאזנה ותלד מפיה, Behold, moreover, among the peculiarities of its nature is this abomination, that the female conceives through the ear and gives birth through the mouth. And Algiahid, inverting this, pretends that Aristotle taught, in the books On the Nature and Properties of Animals, ان الانثي من بنات عرس تلقح من افواهها وتلد من اذانها [inna al-unthī min banāt ʿirs tulqaḥ min afwāhihā wa-talid min ādhānihā] that the females among weasels conceive through the mouth and give birth through the ear. Yet nothing similar occurs in the writings of Aristotle. Indeed, those who idly claim that the weasel gives birth through the mouth he not only refutes but also reveals the origin of the tale, in book 3 On the Generation of Animals, chapter 6. There, after saying that the womb of the weasel is arranged in the same way as that of other quadrupeds, and that the foetus cannot pass from it to the mouth, he adds that this opinion arose διὰ τὸ τίκτειν πάμπαν τὴν γαλῆν σμικρὰ, τῷ δὲ στόματι πολλάκις μεταφέρειν τοὺς νεοττοὺς [dia to tiktein pampan tēn galēn smikra, tō de stomati pollakis metapherein tous neottous], from the fact that the weasel bears very small young, [II, 452] and often carries them about in its mouth. But another explanation presents itself to me, which seems closer to the truth. I think that what the ancients observed in the fish called mustelus [dogfish] was transferred to the weasel. For ὁ γαλεὸς [ho galeos], or the fish mustelus, is also believed to give birth through the mouth. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 55: Ὁ γαλεὸς ὠδίνει διὰ τοῦ στόματος ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ [Ho galeos ōdinei dia tou stomatos en tē thalattē], The mustelus gives birth in the sea through the mouth. [col. 1034] And in book 9, chapter 65: Οἱ μυούμενοι τοῖν Θεοῖν οὐκ ἂν πάσαιντο γαλεοῦ φασιν· οὐ γὰρ εἶναι αὐτὸν καθαρὸν ὄψον ἐπεὶ τῷ στόματι τίκτει [Hoi myoumenoi toin Theoin ouk an pasainto galeou phasin; ou gar einai auton katharon opson epei tō stomati tiktei]. They say that the priests of the Goddesses (namely Ceres and Proserpina) never eat the mustelus fish, for it is not clean food, since it gives birth through the mouth. And it is believed to give birth through the mouth because it sometimes takes its little ones into its mouth, and those who see them coming out imagine this to be a birth. The Philosopher himself touches on this in passing when he says of the mustelus or galeus fishes, in History, book 6, chapter 10: Ἐξαφιᾶσι καὶ δέχονται εἰς ἑαυτοὺς τοὺς νεοττούς [Exaphiasi kai dechontai eis heautous tous neottous]; They take their young back into themselves after letting them out. But others say it much more explicitly. Antigonus, History 25: Τῶν δὲ γαλεῶν τὰ ἔμβρυα, ἐξιόντα ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας, νέμεται· καὶ πάλιν ἐκδύεται (read εἰσδύεται [eisdyetai]) κατὰ τὸ στόμα [Tōn de galeōn ta embrya, exionta ek tēs koilias, nemetai; kai palin ekdyetai … kata to stoma]. The foetuses of the galei, coming out of the womb, feed, and enter again through the mouth. Athenaeus, book 7, chapter 12: Τίκτει δὲ ὁ γαλεὸς τὰ πλεῖστα τρία, καὶ εἰσδέχεται τὰ γεννηθέντα εἰς τὸ στόμα,. καὶ πάλιν ἀφίησι [Tiktei de ho galeos ta pleista tria, kai eisdechetai ta gennēthenta eis to stoma, kai palin aphiēsi]; The mustelus usually bears three young, and takes them into its mouth, and lets them out again. Plutarch says that the young are formed from an egg within the mother's womb itself, and then let out through the mouth as if by a second generation. The words are in the book Utra anim.: Τίκτουσι μὲν γὰρ ὠὸν, εἶτα ζῶον, οὐκ ἐκτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐντὸς ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. καὶ τρέφουσιν οὕτως, καὶ φέρουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐκ δευτέρας γενέσεως [Tiktousi men gar ōon, eita zōon, ouk ektos, alla entos en heautois. kai trephousin houtōs, kai pherousin, hōsper ek deuteras geneseōs]. And in Περὶ Φιλοστοργίας [Peri Philostorgias] he says that they take back those they have let out, and wrap them, as they sleep, in their own entrails: Οἱ γαλεοὶ ζωογονοῦσι μὲν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐκβαίνειν δὲ παρέχουσιν ἐκτὸς, καὶ νέμεσθαι τοῖς σκύμνοις, εἶτα πάλιν ἀναλαμβάνουσι, καὶ περιπτύσσουσιν ἐγκοιμώμενοι τοῖς σπλάγχνοις [Hoi galeoi zōogonousi men en heautois, ekbainein de parechousin ektos, kai nemesthai tois skymnois, eita palin analambanousi, kai periptyssousin enkoimōmenoi tois splanchnois]. Aelian too, book 2, chapter 55: Πάλιν τε εἰσδέχεται τὰ βρέφη, κἀνεμεῖ ταῖς αὐταῖς ὁδοῖς ζῶντα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ [Palin te eisdechetai ta brephē, kanemei tais autais hodois zōnta, kai apathē]; It takes its young back (through the mouth) and by the same way vomits them up again alive and unharmed. That is, it protects them in this way in sudden fear. The same Aelian, book 9, chapter 65: Οὐ τίκτειν δὲ αὐτὸν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν· ἀλλὰ, δείσαντά τι τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων, τὰ σκυλάκια καταπίνειν, καὶ ἀποκρύπτειν. εἶτα τοῦ φοβήσαντος παραδραμόντος, ζῶντα αὖθις ἀνεμεῖν [Ou tiktein de auton enioi legousin; alla, deisanta ti tōn epibouleuontōn, ta skylakia katapinein, kai apokryptein. eita tou phobēsantos paradramontos, zōnta authis anemein]. Some say that it does not give birth through the mouth, but that, struck with fear of some attacker, it swallows its young and hides them; then, when the fear is removed, it vomits them up again alive. Many report the same of the glaucus fish, as the same Aelian, book 1, chapter 16; Oppian, Halieutica, book 1, line 749; Phile, chapter 69. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 4, History 126, writes that the glaucus, the dogfish and the galeus hide their young in fear, the glaucus and the dogfish in the mouth, the galeus in the belly, καὶ πάλιν ταῦτα γεννᾷν, τοῦ φόβου [kai palin tauta gennan, tou phobou] [II, 453] παρελθόντος [parelthontos], and bring them forth again when the fear has passed. Thus from this cloud of witnesses it appears that it is not τὴν γαλῆν [tēn galēn], that is, the four-footed weasel, but τὸν γαλεὸν [ton galeon], that is, the mustelus fish, that emits its young from the mouth; and that this was believed either to be a true birth or to be like a birth. Rightly, therefore, Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3, refutes those who say that the weasel conceives through the ear and pours forth its offspring through the mouth (so it must be read, not, as commonly, conceives through the mouth and through the ear, etc., although the Arabs follow the latter). And many indeed said that the weasel gives birth through the mouth, as we know from the Philosopher. But whether anyone said that it conceives through the ear before Aristeas, I do not know; he seems to have embellished the tale in this way so that the weasel might be a type of informers and slanderers. For these, he says, entangle others in evils, ὅσα διὰ ἀκοῆς λαβόντες, ταῦτα τῷ λόγῳ σωματοποιήσαντες [hosa dia akoēs labontes, tauta tō logō sōmatopoiēsantes], as it were embodying in words what they had received through their ears, that is, exaggerating and magnifying them: which is a new and wholly unusual sense of the verb σωματοποιεῖν [sōmatopoiein]. Barnabas too is mistaken when, in order to fasten on the weasel the horrible crime of fellators, he says not that it gives birth through the mouth but κύειν [kyein], conceives. Ἀλλὰ, he says, καὶ τὴν γαλῆν ἐμίσησε καλῶς. οὐ μὴ γάρ φησιν, ὁμοιωθήσῃ τοῖς τοιούτοις, οἵους ἀκούομεν ἀνομίαν ποιοῦντας τῷ στόματι, διὰ ἀκαθαρσίαν, etc. Τὸ γὰρ ζῶον τοῦτο τῷ στόματι κύει [Alla … kai tēn galēn emisēse kalōs. ou mē gar phēsin, homoiōthēsē tois toioutois, hoious akouomen anomian poiountas tō stomati, dia akatharsian … To gar zōon touto tō stomati kyei]. Therefore we do not think anything should be changed in that passage; nor in this respect do we agree [col. 1035] with the opinion of a most excellent and most learned man, and a very dear friend of ours, who in his Notes on this Epistle (how learned they are!) holds that this passage is corrupt and must be restored from Aristeas. The Egyptians also wanted the weasels to be an example of the lewdness of tribades, as Horapollo teaches, Hieroglyphica, book 2, chapter 34; but others, more decent, in Plutarch's Isis, hold that τὴν γαλῆν κατὰ τὸ οὖς ὀχευομένην, τῷ δὲ στόματι τίκτουσαν, εἴκασμα τῆς τοῦ λόγου γενέσεως εἶναι [tēn galēn kata to ous ocheuomenēn, tō de stomati tiktousan, eikasma tēs tou logou geneseōs einai], the weasel, since it is covered through the ear and gives birth through the mouth, represents the generation of speech.
